parts.title: Study guides for students
parts.instructions: Read what each person is looking for. Match each person to the best text. There are three extra texts.

people.text: Ravi finds it hard to concentrate at home. He wants a quiet place where he can work for several hours without being disturbed.
Amy has to learn many dates and facts for her history exam. She would like a tip that helps her to remember things more easily.
Stefan always feels nervous before exams and cannot sleep the night before. He would like advice to feel calmer.
Lucia needs to practise her speaking for an English test. She wants someone to talk with and correct her mistakes.
Omar often leaves everything until the last minute. He needs a plan that shows him what to study each day.

texts.title: Make a Timetable
texts.text: Write down every subject and divide your time into short sessions with breaks. Stick it on your wall.

texts.title: Use Flashcards
texts.text: Write questions on one side and answers on the other. Test yourself often to fix facts in your memory.

texts.title: Join a Study Group
texts.text: Working with friends can be fun, but you must stay focused on the work.

texts.title: Find a Speaking Partner
texts.text: Practise with a friend or teacher. Ask them to point out your mistakes.

texts.title: Stay Calm
texts.text: Breathe slowly, go for a walk and go to bed early. Try not to study late at night before the exam.

texts.title: Go to the Library
texts.text: Libraries are quiet, so you can work for hours without noise.

texts.title: Eat Well
texts.text: A healthy breakfast helps you think clearly in the morning.

texts.title: Read Past Papers
texts.text: Look at old exams to learn what the questions are like.

parts.title: Exam day
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
On the morning of my final maths exam, I woke up at six o'clock, an hour before my alarm. My heart was beating fast and I could not eat any breakfast. My mother made me a cup of tea and told me, 'You've done everything you can. Now just do your best.'

When I reached school, the corridor was full of students looking at their notes. Some were whispering formulas, and others were silently staring at the walls. I decided not to look at my notes any more, because I thought it would only make me more nervous. Instead, I talked to my friend Dani about football.

In the exam hall, the teacher gave out the papers and told us we could begin. For a moment, I could not read the first question because my hands were shaking. Then I took a deep breath, and the numbers started to make sense. I worked carefully for two hours, and I even had ten minutes left to check my answers.

When I walked out, I felt tired but relieved. I do not know my result yet, but I know I tried my best. My mother was right.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer not eat breakfast?
questions.explanation: His heart was beating fast and he could not eat.

questions.prompt: What did the writer do in the corridor?
questions.explanation: He talked to Dani about football.

questions.prompt: What happened when the exam began?
questions.explanation: For a moment he could not read because his hands were shaking.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel at the end?
questions.explanation: He felt tired but relieved.

questions.prompt: What does the writer think about his mother's advice?
questions.explanation: He says "My mother was right."

parts.title: Revising for exams
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every year, thousands of students feel worried as exams get closer, but a few simple habits can help. [1] Many students try to study for six hours without a break, but this is not a good idea.

It is better to work for forty minutes and then rest for ten. [2] Walk around, drink some water or listen to music for a short time.

Another useful idea is to explain what you have learnt to someone else. [3] If you cannot explain it, you probably need to study it again.

Sleep is also very important. [4] Your brain needs rest to remember what you have studied. [5] Finally, remember that one exam does not decide your future.
sentences: You may be surprised how much you remember.
Do not stay up late studying the night before the test.
First, make a plan that includes regular breaks.
Use this time to do something relaxing.
Some exams are held in July and others in January.
Try to keep calm and be proud of your effort.

gaps.explanation: A plan with breaks introduces the topic of studying without breaks.
The relaxing activities listed after the gap fit "use this time to do something relaxing".
"You may be surprised how much you remember" fits after explaining things to others.
Staying up late is the opposite of the importance of sleep, and the next sentence gives the reason.
The final advice about staying calm leads naturally to "one exam does not decide your future".

parts.title: A talk about studying
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: helen
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Today I'm going to give you some advice about studying for exams. My first tip is to find a quiet place. Many students prefer the library, but a bedroom can work too. Second, switch off your phone, because it is a big distraction. Third, study for about forty minutes and then take a break for ten. During your break, have a glass of water or a piece of fruit. The best time to study is in the morning, when your head is fresh. Finally, you should get at least eight hours of sleep. I know that sounds like a lot, but it makes a big difference. There will be a revision class on Tuesday, so please come if you need extra help.

gaps.explanation: My first tip is to find a quiet place.
Switch off your phone, because it is a distraction.

gaps.explanation: Have a glass of water or a piece of fruit.

gaps.explanation: The best time to study is in the morning.

parts.title: A student
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Today I'm speaking to Jenna, who has just finished her final school exams. Jenna, how did you feel on the first day?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Terrible! I'd hardly slept, and my stomach felt strange. But after the first twenty minutes, I relaxed.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: How did you prepare?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: I made a timetable in March, so I wasn't in a hurry. I studied one subject each evening and wrote summaries on coloured paper.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: Was there a subject that you found difficult?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Physics. I didn't understand it at first, so my brother explained it to me. He's very patient.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What did you do to relax?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: I went running every afternoon. It cleared my mind, and then I could study again with energy.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What was the hardest part of the whole experience?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: Waiting for the results. It took six weeks, and I thought about it every day.

turns.speaker: gerard
turns.text: What are you going to do now?

turns.speaker: jenna
turns.text: I'm going to travel for a few months, and then I'll go to university to study biology.
